title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative / Testability Failure under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered unique intent→configuration tasks in a paired design contrasting (a) baseline LLM-only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic validator). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) and model_calls_used = 200. Observed (confirmatory set): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Paired SAFE-rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). Because identical per-pair generations were produced and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was mechanically untestable in this execution. We (1) publish the complete preregistered run and core artifacts (execution/*, analysis/*), (2) provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of the testability failure tied to three archived facts (shared generation semantics, validator labels, absence of repairs), and (3) give concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations—independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the preregistered exploratory reserve, pilot checks before confirmatory commitment, and explicit repair instrumentation—to enable informative repeats.

sections.introduction: Automated translation from human intent to device configuration using large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency gains in network operations (NetOps). At the same time, an erroneous configuration change can cause outages or security exposures. Tool‑augmentation—coupling an LLM generator to deterministic validators or sandboxed simulators in a generate–validate–repair architecture—is widely proposed to reduce operational risk. We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) to quantify whether adding a deterministic verifier causally reduces verifier‑detected unsafe proposals produced by a hosted LLM for synthetic intent→configuration tasks. The preregistration specified a paired binary estimand (guarded − baseline SAFE rate), a paired exact McNemar two‑sided test with bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples, seed = 1729), N=200 tasks, explicit exclusion/missingness rules, and two permitted generation semantics (independent per‑arm generation or shared_initial_candidate). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate semantics to conserve hosted model budget. The confirmatory outcome was degenerate: every sampled candidate was labeled SAFE by the deterministic validator in both arms (n11 = 200, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0), producing a paired estimate of 0.0 and p = 1.0. This paper does not claim verifier efficacy from that null/ceiling outcome. Instead, we (a) expose, with archived artifact evidence, why the executed design was non‑informative for the preregistered estimand; (b) present reproducible diagnostics grounded in execution and analysis artifacts; and (c) offer artifact‑supported, operationally concrete recommendations for informative repeats. Our contribution is methodological: a fully archived preregistered run, a precise diagnosis of a testability failure mechanism, and clear design changes to restore inferential testability while preserving the original scientific question.
sections.related_work: Recent surveys and prototype reports document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration generation, diagnostic assistance) while emphasizing safety and evaluation challenges [1,2,3]. A common finding is that augmenting LLMs with external deterministic tools—validators, schema‑enforcers, or sandbox simulators—often improves measured correctness on curated tasks, but reported gains are sensitive to verifier fidelity and evaluation semantics [4,5]. Method papers advocating generate–validate–refine or divide–verify–refine pipelines spell out desiderata for workflow‑centred, replayable evaluations with explicit initial/final state semantics and archived validator traces [6,2]. Work on guardrails, schema interfaces, and agent orchestration highlights operational trade‑offs: stricter checks can lower unsafe accepts but increase false refusals and operator workload unless ROC‑style diagnostics are collected [3,7]. Our study adopts the workflow‑centred, preregistered, sandboxed evaluation practices advocated in that literature and directly addresses an empirical gap: reproducible, preregistered adversarial NetOps experiments that quantify the paired causal effect of deterministic verification under clearly declared generation semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study was preregistered as cand-2026-01-prereg-v1. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) on binary SAFE indicators from a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar (paired_binary_analysis_v1). Confidence intervals: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistration specified N=200 paired tasks, power assumptions (target detect ≈7 percentage‑point paired reduction), and explicit admissible deviations and stopping rules.

Task generator, scope, and seeds. A deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to single‑AS, multi‑device topologies and limited fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Each task manifest includes initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, difficulty metadata, and a per‑task generation_seed. The preregistration partitioned tasks into benign and adversarial prompt transforms using a templated obfuscation rule set; an exploratory reserve of up to 50 tasks was preregistered for adversarial calibration.

Pipelines and generation semantics. Baseline: post‑hoc scoring of the LLM candidate (no runtime enforcement) using deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded: the same LLM candidate validated in a deterministic sandbox by deterministic_netops_validator_v5; repairs were permitted by design (one repair call per task) but in the confirmatory episodes no repair traces were recorded. The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: independent per‑arm generation (two model calls per task) or shared_initial_candidate (one shared model call per task scored by both arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate to conserve model calls; model_calls_used = 200 (execution manifest).

Scoring and analysis. The deterministic validator applied full_intent_constraint_validation and emitted deterministic valid flags and detailed traces (validation_before/after, violation lists). Confirmatory binary outcomes derived from validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to compute contingency counts, exact McNemar p, and paired bootstrap CI (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). The preregistered missingness and exclusion rules (duplicate prompts, nondeterministic verifier behavior, technical failures) were applied automatically; none triggered in the confirmatory set.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and basic facts. The archived execution manifest reports completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200, consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. Provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200; no cross‑condition cache reuse was observed. Deterministic reconciliation checks passed: complete_pair_count = 200; baseline_success_count = 200; guarded_success_count = 200; n11 = 200; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory candidate as valid: baseline SAFE = 200/200 and guarded SAFE = 200/200. The paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) equals 0.0. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test produced p = 1.0. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI is degenerate at [0.0, 0.0] (resamples = 10000; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These numerical results are identical to archived analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) and to the paired_binary_analysis_v1 outputs.

Representative traces and repair instrumentation. Representative scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) show shared_initial_candidate contents identical across baseline and guarded episodes, validator.validation_before/after with violation_count = 0, and validator.valid = true. repair_provider_trace fields are null in all confirmatory scoring records, confirming that no automatic repair was invoked in these episodes. The absence of repair events implies the guarded arm performed pure validation only; no repaired candidate produced discordance.

Missingness, contamination, and exploratory reserve. analysis/missingness_summary.csv records complete_pairs = 200 and no failed or unscorable episodes. analysis/contamination_summary.csv shows no flagged episodes. The preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) intended for ROC/refusal calibration was not consumed prior to confirmatory execution; therefore no ROC or refusal diagnostics were produced for the confirmatory set.
sections.discussion:
Why the inferential test was uninformative. The inferential degeneracy is attributable to three archived facts, each independently verifiable in the bundle: (1) generation semantics: the run executed shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false) so only one LLM candidate per task was generated and shared across both arms (see execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json); (2) validator outcomes: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every sampled candidate as valid in both arms (see execution/scoring/*.json and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv); and (3) absence of repairs: repair_provider_trace is null in the confirmatory scoring JSONs, so the guarded arm did not alter any shared candidates. Together these facts mechanically prevent discordant paired outcomes (n10 or n01 > 0), which McNemar's test requires to assess a paired effect. Crucially, a ceiling of SAFE labels does not constitute evidence that the guarded pipeline would reduce unsafe proposals under alternative semantics or distributions; it reveals a testability failure under the chosen execution semantics and sampled model behaviour.

Interpretation relative to preregistered power assumptions. The preregistration's power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (~10–15%) and a detectable discordant proportion; those assumptions were not borne out. The executed shared semantics reduced per‑arm sampling variability and thus the opportunity for discordance. Independent per‑arm generation (the preregistered alternative) would have required roughly 200 additional model calls (400 total) and could have produced arm‑level stochasticity necessary to reveal an effect. The arithmetic trade‑off linking required model calls to estimand testability is explicit in the preregistration and execution manifests.

Design recommendations to restore testability (artifact‑grounded). All recommendations follow directly from the preregistration and execution artifacts and are implementable without inventing new infrastructure:
- Use independent per‑arm generation for confirmatory paired contrasts unless the guarded arm will deterministically repair candidates in a way that guarantees discordance; this restores arm‑specific stochasticity and requires increasing model_calls to the preregistered maximum (≈400).
- Before committing to the full confirmatory set, consume the preregistered exploratory reserve (≤50 tasks) to calibrate adversarial transforms so the baseline unsafe rate matches power assumptions; archive these calibration runs and lock transform parameters before confirmatory execution.
- If repairs are permitted in the guarded pipeline, instrument and archive repair_provider_trace artifacts and report the UNSAFE→SAFE conversion rate as a primary diagnostic; this both creates discordance potential and quantifies repair utility and safety.
- Implement a deterministic pilot check that computes contingency counts on a small holdout; if the pilot produces a ceiling/floor contingency, apply a preregistered contingency‑preserving adaptation (e.g., enable independent draws or intensify adversarial transforms) rather than proceeding with an uninformative confirmatory test.

Threats to validity and external generalization. Internal validity: under shared_generation semantics the paired estimand conflates generator sampling policy with verifier effect; independent per‑arm draws are needed to separate these factors. Construct validity: the deterministic validator encodes full_intent_constraint_validation for the synthetic task family (admin/mtu/vlan); its completeness with respect to production failure modes is limited. External validity: synthetic single‑AS topologies and a single model (gpt-5-mini) constrain generalizability. Conclusion validity: the absence of discordant pairs removes inferential power—statistical tests cannot distinguish classifier behavior when discordance is absent. These limitations are documented and traceable in the archived artifacts (execution/*, analysis/*).
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing a hosted LLM (declared model: gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic verifier pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and for the sampled LLM outputs, both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This ceiling outcome was a testability failure for the preregistered causal estimand rather than evidence of the validator's efficacy in broader settings. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts that permit deterministic replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis tying the uninformative outcome to shared generation semantics, universal SAFE labels, and absent repairs; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration via the preregistered exploratory reserve, pilot contingency checks, and repair instrumentation) to enable informative repeats. Investigators re-running or extending this study should inspect the archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution/* and analysis/*) and adopt the recommended design changes before re‑executing confirmatory tests. The archived bundle contains all inputs, scoring traces, and analysis outputs needed to replay and audit the run and to implement the recommended repeat protocol.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt-5-mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
